item.content:encoded:
This year's World Series will have a tough act to follow. Not only was the 2025 World Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Toronto Blue Jays the first seven-game affair since 2019, but it featured an 18-inning game and then a Game 7 that might have been the greatest baseball game ever played.
The good news is we're guaranteed that a long-starved fanbase will get to celebrate in 2026. The Milwaukee Brewers, coming off their impressive and dynamic four-game sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, are in the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982 and seek the first championship in franchise history, looking to put an exclamation point on their season after leading the majors with 103 wins.
The Tampa Bay Rays were a 1998 expansion franchise and reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020 (the shortened season during the COVID-19 pandemic) but are seeking their first title as well. Young power hitter Junior Caminero and unheralded staff ace Drew Rasmussen lead the way as the Rays look to finally cash in after making the playoffs six times in the past eight seasons.
The Brewers and Rays led their respective leagues in wins, always a bonus for those who want the best teams in the World Series. Of course, a lot of attention will be given to the small-market aspect of the matchup, as the cloud of the lockout looms in the offseason.
Let's rank all the World Series since 2000 to see where Brewers-Rays fits in. This ranking is based on hype, the quality of the teams and their star power heading into the World Series. It's not a ranking of the quality of the World Series itself, although we're going to include a grade on that for each matchup. Let's get to it.
The Yankees were back in the World Series for the sixth time in eight years, and the Marlins had rebuilt after their fire sale following their World Series title in 1997. Trust me when I say that nobody wanted the Yankees in the World Series yet again. And the Marlins were merely a 91-win wild-card team. Most notably, however, both teams had spoiled the ultimate World Series by knocking off the Cubs and Red Sox -- before either team had overcome its curse -- in Game 7s in the LCS.
Actual World Series: C. The Marlins won Game 4 in 12 innings, when Yankees manager Joe Torre inexplicably failed to use reliever Mariano Rivera, and then 23-year-old Josh Beckett tossed a five-hit shutout in Game 6.
In an all-wild-card series, the fifth-seeded Rangers had won 90 games and the sixth-seeded Diamondbacks won only 84, making this the lowest combined win total in World Series history (for full seasons). The Rangers were going for their first World Series title, so there was that, and there were some fun hitters -- Corey Seager, the red-hot Adolis Garcia (who had just driven in 15 runs in the ALCS) and Corbin Carroll -- but it was a soft matchup on paper.
Actual World Series: D-. The series turned on Seager's tying two-run homer off Paul Sewald in the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, which Garcia then won with a home run in the 11th. There wasn't a single lead change after that, and three of those games were blowouts.
This was the Cardinals team that got hot in September and clinched a wild-card spot on the final day of the season when the Braves blew a lead in the ninth inning and lost in extra innings. St. Louis certainly had star power with the likes of Albert Pujols, Lance Berkman and Matt Holliday but had won a World Series fairly recently (2006), and the Rangers had just been there the year before.
Actual World Series: A. The first two games were one-run games, including the Rangers pulling out a victory with two runs in the ninth. In Game 3, Pujols blasted a record-tying three home runs. Game 6 was the David Freese Game -- perhaps the single most exciting baseball game ever played. Game 7 was a bit of an anticlimactic 6-2 Cardinals win.
The second-lowest combined win total in World Series history featured two wild-card teams that won fewer than 90 games. The Royals were at least a good story -- in the playoffs for the first time since winning the World Series in 1985 -- and had gone 8-0 in the AL playoffs, including an epic win over the A's in the wild-card game. The Giants, however, had just won the World Series in 2010 and 2012, and this team didn't seem nearly as good as those two.
Actual World Series: B-. Five of the games were blowouts, but it did at least go seven. It'll be remembered for Madison Bumgarner's historic performance: a shutout in Game 5 (the last complete game shutout in World Series history) and then five scoreless innings of relief in Game 7, getting Salvador Perez to pop out with the tying run on third to end it.
The Red Sox were only three years removed from breaking the Curse of the Bambino in 2004, so although they were still a star-laden team with David Ortiz, Manny Ramirez and scrappy rookie Dustin Pedroia, they were no longer as interesting. The Rockies were a fun story, winning 14 of their final 15 games, including beating the Padres in a tiebreaker, just to win a wild-card spot. Then they went 7-0 in the NL playoffs and had won 21 of 22 entering the World Series.
Actual World Series: F.A dud. Two of the games were one-run games, but this goes down as one of the least memorable World Series of all time, with a forgettable four-game sweep.
The Tigers were the story of the season. They had lost 119 games three years before and 91 just the previous year. With rookie starter Justin Verlander winning 17 games, they led the AL Central most of the season -- only to lose their final five games and squeak into the playoffs as a wild-card team. The Cardinals won a weak NL Central with only 83 wins -- although they at least had Pujols at his absolute peak (.331/.431/.671, 49 home runs). Both teams hadn't won a World Series in a couple of decades: 1982 for the Cardinals, 1984 for the Tigers. Plus, it did feature two of the original 16 franchises.
Actual World Series: F. The Cardinals won one game in the bottom of the eighth, but it was otherwise a blur of nothing, most characterized by several fielding miscues by Tigers pitchers. David Eckstein won MVP honors without hitting a home run and while driving in only four runs.
The Braves were back in the World Series for the first time since 1999 -- they had made 12 playoff appearances in the intervening years without making it to the Fall Classic. Still, this was the weakest of the Atlanta playoff teams of recent vintage, winning only 88 games and missing Ronald Acuña Jr. for the playoffs. The Astros, meanwhile, were back in the World Series for the third time in five years -- but the first time since the 2017 sign-stealing scandal had broken in November 2019. Let's just say not everyone wanted them there.
Actual World Series: D. This was a weird World Series. The Braves ended up going with two bullpen games (who remembers that Dylan Lee and Tucker Davidson started?) after Charlie Morton broke a leg in Game 1. Astros starters kept getting knocked out early (the only starter to go more than five innings for either team was Max Fried in the finale). Four of the games were blowouts.
The Giants were back after winning in 2010, and the Tigers were back for the first time since 2006, featuring Triple Crown winner Miguel Cabrera and a strong 1-2 punch in the rotation with Verlander and Max Scherzer. This was also the last World Series with that season's MVP winners until Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani in 2024, with Cabrera and Buster Posey.
Actual World Series: D-. A boring sweep. Pablo Sandoval did hit three home runs in Game 1, but there were two shutouts and chilly weather in Detroit made the final two games unbearable.
This one did feature the two best teams from the regular season (both won 97 games), the last time before this year that we had that happen in a full season. It was also a classic original-16 matchup, although we had seen this in 2004 -- plus, both teams had won recently (2007 for Boston, 2011 for St. Louis). These were veteran teams, with Ortiz leading the Red Sox and the Cardinals featuring four .300 hitters, plus Carlos Beltran, who hit .296 and led the team in home runs.
Actual World Series: C+. Ortiz was absolutely locked in, hitting .688/.760/1.188 with two home runs and eight walks. The Cardinals were so scared of him by Game 6 that they intentionally walked him three times -- with two of those helping lead to rallies and a 6-1 Red Sox victory in the final game.
This one could be No. 25 -- it was during the pandemic, after all, and it was played at a neutral site in a half-empty stadium for social distancing reasons. But it was a great matchup between the teams with the best records in each league, albeit over the shortened 60-game season. You had Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw and Randy Arozarena in the midst of one of the best postseasons ever, plus the small-market Rays trying to beat the big-market Dodgers.
Actual World Series: C+. Because teams were allowed an expanded roster of 28 players, it was a parade of relievers -- but there were some fun games, including a bonkers ending to Game 4 and then Rays manager Kevin Cash's controversial decision to remove Blake Snell in Game 6, which backfired in a big way.
Maybe this should rate higher. After all, at the time, the White Sox were trying to break a World Series drought going back to 1917 and the Astros, born in 1962, had never won. But the White Sox's drought never had the same nationwide interest as the ones for the Cubs or Red Sox (fair or not) and these weren't particularly interesting teams. The White Sox were very good -- they won 99 games -- but lacked star power, with Paul Konerko their biggest name (Frank Thomas was on the team that year but played only 34 games and was injured for the playoffs). The Astros had Yankees transplants Roger Clemens and Andy Pettitte, but their two longtime stars, Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, were at the end of their careers (Bagwell, in his final season, was relegated to DH and pinch-hitting duties).
Actual World Series: C. It's hard to give a sweep a decent grade, but all four games were exciting, including Scott Podsednik's walk-off home run in Game 2 (after not hitting a home run all season) and Geoff Blum's go-ahead home run in the 14th inning to win Game 3.
The Phillies were back in the World Series for the first time since 1993 -- and hadn't won since 1980. They featured a powerful offense with Chase Utley, Ryan Howard, Jimmy Rollins and Pat Burrell. The Rays were maybe the unlikeliest World Series team ever: In their 10 previous years of existence, they had not only never had a winning season but had lost at least 90 games in each one. They won 97 games that year behind rookie Evan Longoria and power-hitting first baseman Carlos Peña, with speedsters Carl Crawford and B.J. Upton in the outfield.
Actual World Series: D+. Three games were decided by one run, but it was a pretty uneventful World Series. The lasting memory is the cold and rain in Philly that forced the midgame postponement of Game 5, the only time that has happened in World Series history. The game was suspended in the sixth inning and resumed two days later.
A Subway Series -- the first since the Yankees and Brooklyn Dodgers met in 1956 -- was certainly fun for the Big Apple, but it was less fun for the rest of the country (it drew the worst TV ratings at the time). The Yankees were going for a third straight World Series and had officially become the Evil Empire by that point. To make it even worse, they weren't even that good that season, winning only 87 games. The Mets were back in the World Series for the first time since 1986. There was certainly plenty of star power all around with the likes of Derek Jeter, Roger Clemens and Mike Piazza.
Actual World Series: C+. It was a tight-fought five-game series with all games decided by two runs or fewer. The turning point was the bottom of the ninth of Game 1, when the Yankees tied it off Armando Benitez and went on to win in 12 innings. Game 2 featured the infamous Clemens-Piazza bat-throwing incident, and the Yankees won the clincher with two runs in the ninth off a tired Al Leiter.
I know, the Astros ... again. Boo. But this was an absolute powerhouse of a team with 106 wins and stars such asYordan Alvarez (1.019 OPS) and Verlander (18-4, 1.75 ERA), plus the old standbys Jose Altuve and Alex Bregman. The Phillies, meanwhile, snuck in as a wild-card team for their first playoff trip since 2011 but were an immensely entertaining team with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber& Co., as well as a passionate fanbase cheering them on.
Actual World Series: C. The Phillies won 6-5 in Game 1 on J.T. Realmuto's home run in the 10th inning. They took a 2-1 series lead, but then their bats died. Astros pitchers tossed a combined no-hitter to even the series, and Houston won the final two games 3-2 and 4-1, with Alvarez's three-run blast in Game 6 the deciding blow.
The Brewers' drought is the big narrative here as they try to finally cash in after their past decade of success, but we're still getting the 103-win Brewers facing the 98-win Rays, the best combined win total in the World Series since the Astros and Dodgers in 2017. (Not to mention we get a first-time winner no matter the outcome.) The Brewers aren't your conventional powerhouse team -- relying on speed, defense, timely hitting and a dominant bullpen -- but they do have one of the biggest stars of the 2026 season in Jacob Misiorowski, plus a rising star in young Jackson Chourio. The Rays might lack big names, although Junior Caminero is just the second player with two 40-homer seasons by age 22, and like the Brewers, they're trying to finally win it all after years of success.
Actual World Series: To be determined.
The Royals proved their 2014 World Series appearance was no fluke, winning 95 games with a better team that included trade deadline additions Ben Zobrist and Johnny Cueto. The Mets won the NL East behind a young, powerful rotation that featured Matt Harvey, Noah Syndergaard and Jacob deGrom. It was a fun matchup of teams trying to avoid lengthy title droughts -- 30 years for the Royals, 29 for the Mets.
Actual World Series: C+. It went only five games, but the Royals won the opener in 14 innings, won Game 5 with a three-run eighth inning and then won the clincher in 12 innings -- after Mets manager Terry Collins' ill-fated decision to leave in Harvey to start the ninth with a 2-0 lead.
This was a super entertaining showdown at the time. The Giants had yet to win a World Series in San Francisco and featured Tim Lincecum ("The Freak," for his small stature and overpowering stuff) and two rookies named Posey and Bumgarner. The Rangers had never won a championship and featured AL MVP Josh Hamilton and veteran DH Vladimir Guerrero. Both teams had pulled off upsets in the LCS, with the Giants beating the Phillies and the Rangers beating the Yankees.
Actual World Series: D. Meh. The Giants won the opener in a blowout as the Rangers made four errors and then tossed shutouts in Games 2 (behind Matt Cain) and 4 (behind Bumgarner). You can test Giants fans by asking them who won World Series MVP honors that year. Answer: Edgar Renteria (he hit .412 with two home runs and six RBIs).
Remember, this happened before the sign-stealing scandal changed how we view this era of the Astros. They had won 107 games behind the pitching duo of Verlander and Gerrit Cole and four players who mashed 30-plus home runs (which didn't even include Alvarez, a rookie that year). The Nationals were a wild-card team that had overcome a 19-31 season start to win 93 games and featured a starting pitching trio of Scherzer, Stephen Strasburg and Patrick Corbin (and 20-year-old sensation Juan Soto, who hit 34 home runs).
Actual World Series: B-. It went seven games -- the road team would win all seven -- although five of the games weren't close. The best game was the last one: The Nationals went ahead 3-2 in the seventh inning on Anthony Rendon's home run and then Howie Kendrick's go-ahead home run just inside the right-field foul pole.
This matchup began with a lot of hype: Shohei Ohtani, coming off his all-time game in the NLCS in which he hit three home runs and struck out 10 batters as the starting pitcher, against Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who had hit .442 with six home runs through the first two rounds of the playoffs. The Dodgers were looking to become the first team with back-to-back titles since the 2000 Yankees and the first NL team since the 1976 Reds. The Blue Jays were back in the World Series for the first time since Joe Carter walked off the Phillies in 1993. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts stirred things up after the NLCS when he said during the postgame celebration, "Let's get four more wins and really ruin baseball" -- a reference to the criticism of the Dodgers' high payroll.
Actual World Series: A+. The Dodgers won Game 3 in 18 innings on Freddie Freeman's walk-off home run, which followed an unlikely four-inning relief performance from Will Klein, the last guy on the Dodgers' staff. The Dodgers went back to Toronto trailing 3-2 but won Game 6 behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto and a crazy game-ending double play.
Game 7 featured two future Hall of Famers starting in Ohtani and Max Scherzer, more on-the-edge-of-your-seat plays than any game in World Series history, Miguel Rojas' unlikely home run in the ninth to tie it, as well as Will Smith's go-ahead one in the 11th -- and finally, Yamamoto pitching in relief to close out the game by inducing a double play with two runners on to win it for the Dodgers. It wasn't quite the greatest World Series overall, but two all-time games made it a classic.
The Angels, who joined the majors in 1961, were making their first World Series appearance, while the Giants, in the Bay Area since 1958, were trying to win their first title since moving from New York. You had Barry Bonds at the height of his unstoppable powers -- and trying to erase his own postseason demons -- while the Angels had a loaded lineup (Troy Glaus, Tim Salmon, Garret Anderson), the Rally Monkey and those deafening ThunderStix (let us pray they never return).
Actual World Series: A. Bonds was a beast, hitting .471/.700/1.294 (yes, that's a 1.994 OPS), but it wasn't enough. This series featured four one-run games, including a wild 11-10 contest and the classic Game 6, when the Angels rallied late from a 5-0 deficit to win 6-5. Game 7 was a drab 4-1 contest (Bonds went a harmless 1-for-3).
The Yankees had missed the playoffs in 2008 for the first time since 1993, so they went out and signed free agents CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett to add to an already stacked roster that included Jeter, Alex Rodriguez, Robinson Cano, Hideki Matsui, Jorge Posada and Johnny Damon. Whoa. Yes, they were still the Evil Empire. The Phillies, trying to defend their title, had traded for Cliff Lee and then signed Pedro Martinez in July to bolster their rotation.
Actual World Series: C. It could have been a classic battle, but there were no one-run games and Game 6 -- Martinez's final start of his career -- was over early. The crucial contest was Game 4, when the Yankees scored three runs in the ninth off Phillies closer Brad Lidge to win 7-4.
This one presented conflicting emotions. The Yankees were going for an unthinkable fourth straight title, but in the wake of 9/11, there was a "Win it for New York" angle that the Yankees had never encountered. The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, had the big, bad duo of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling. When asked on the eve of the World Series about the Yankees' mystique and aura, Schilling provided one of the great quips in World Series history: "Mystique and Aura? Those are dancers at a nightclub." The Diamondbacks were not going to be intimidated.
Actual World Series: A+. Four one-run games, including three of the most memorable World Series moments ever: Jeter's Mr. November home run to win Game 4, Scott Brosius' walk-off home run to win Game 5 and then Luis Gonzalez's bloop single to beat the invincible Mariano Rivera in Game 7.
Two of baseball's most historic franchises had never met in a World Series, creating the classic showdown with games in Fenway Park and Dodger Stadium. It doesn't get any better than that. The Red Sox were a 108-win powerhouse -- with AL MVP Mookie Betts leading the way, backed up by J.D. Martinez, who hit .330 with 43 home runs that season. Chris Sale and David Price headlined the rotation. The Dodgers actually had a bit of a down year with 92 wins, but they also weren't lacking in big names, with Manny Machado (a trade deadline acquisition), Yasiel Puig, Matt Kemp, Cody Bellinger and Justin Turner, with Kershaw and rookie Walker Buehler on the pitching side.
Actual World Series: C-. A letdown. The first two games in Fenway were cold and windy. Game 3 was an 18-inning affair -- the longest in World Series history -- but was more of a slog than a game to remember. Game 4 was the best of the series as the Red Sox rallied with nine runs over the final three innings to win 9-6.
This series had it all: dominant teams (both won over 100 games), long World Series title droughts (never for the Astros, 1988 for the Dodgers) and superstars galore (Altuve, Verlander, Carlos Correa, Kershaw, Seager, Bellinger, Yu Darvish). We didn't know at the time that both franchises were just kicking off 100-win dynasties -- let alone what the Astros were doing behind the scenes -- but the anticipation level was off the charts for the first matchup of 100-win teams in the World Series since 1970.
Actual World Series: A-. Game 1, with a start-time temperature of 103 degrees at Dodger Stadium, was a Kershaw 11-strikeout gem. The Astros tied Game 2 in the ninth on Marwin Gonzalez's home run off Kenley Jansen (1.32 ERA that season), both teams scored twice in the 10th, the Astros scored twice in the 11th on George Springer's home run and held on for a 7-6 win. Game 4 featured a five-run rally in the ninth by the Dodgers to win. Game 5 was completely bananas, with the Astros finally winning 13-12 in 10 innings. Game 7 was a letdown though, as the Astros won a 5-1 snoozer in which they scored five runs off Darvish in the first two innings.
As mentioned, what's not to like? Aside from Ohtani and Judge each playing in their first World Series and trying to put a final stamp on their legacy-defining seasons, we hadJuan Soto and Mookie Betts, a suddenly rejuvenated Giancarlo Stanton and a hobbled Freddie Freeman (only raising the drama if he hit well), Gerrit Cole and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Aside from the history between the clubs, we had both clubs needing to rewrite their recent history: The Yankees, back in the World Series for the first time since 2009, and the Dodgers trying to add a more legitimate championship to the one they won in the COVID-shortened season.
Actual World Series:C+. The Judge-Ohtani showdown was a flop, as Judge hit .222 with one home run and Ohtani hit .105 without a home run or RBI. The series also went just five games, with the Dodgers winning the first three. The series did produce two forever moments, however: Freeman's walk-off, Kirk Gibson-esque grand slam in Game 1 and the Yankees' fifth-inning defensive meltdown in Game 5.
The Red Sox were coming off their never-done-before comeback from down 3-0 to beat the Yankees in the ALCS -- and still had to beat a 105-win Cardinals team that featured Pujols (.331, 46 home runs), Jim Edmonds (.301, 42 home runs) and Scott Rolen (.314, 34 home runs), plus in-season pickup Larry Walker, who had an OPS over 1.000 that year. The Red Sox had their own ridiculous lineup with Ortiz (.301, 41 home runs), Ramirez (.308, 43 home runs) and Damon (.304, 20 home runs) plus a rotation with Schilling and Martinez. It seems inevitable now that Boston was going to win, but that wasn't the case at the time, so the buildup was intense.
Actual World Series: D. Blah. I mean, Red Sox fans will rightfully call it the best World Series ever, but after a sloppy 11-9 Game 1 played in a drizzle at Fenway (the Red Sox won despite committing four errors), the Cardinals never led again.
The Cubs had not only not won since 1908, but they hadn't even been in a World Series since 1945. The Guardians, meanwhile, had the second-longest drought of the original 16 teams, without a title since 1948. That was enough right there to build up the anticipation, but this also rates high because it was two good teams -- Chicago won 104 games while Cleveland won 94. Cubs third baseman Kris Bryant won MVP honors that year and Cleveland was led by 18-game winner Corey Kluber (who would start three times) and young rising stars Francisco Lindor and Jose Ramirez.
Actual World Series: B. The first six games weren't anything too special, but Game 7 was one of the greatest in World Series history. Cleveland tied it on Rajai Davis' three-run homer in the bottom of the eighth, the Cubs scored twice in the 10th -- following a stress-filled rain delay -- and escaped with an 8-7, curse-ending win when Cleveland had to bat little-used Michael Martinez with its season on the line.

item.content:encoded:
MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point.
What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according to FanSided's Robert Murray) with projected contracts and destinations.
LHP Tarik Skubal
Projected deal: 9 years, $378 million ($42 million AAV) with New York Mets
Regardless of how CBA negotiations shake out, Tarik Skubal's long-rumored $400 million price tag may ultimately prove to be an overestimation. There's a reason no pitcher has ever received such a paycheck, Shohei Ohtani notwithstanding. Still, Skubal should become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history. His durability, both in-game and season-long, combined with razor-sharp stuff in the prime of his career, should give teams the confidence to invest in Skubal over an extended period.
The Dodgers are the natural landing spot after acquiring him at the trade deadline, but the Mets are baseball's richest team and there's mounting pressure for New York to start competing, in a serious way, with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor. Skubal is the ultimate floor-raiser in a rotation, and he'd form a mean one-two punch with breakout ace Nolan McLean.
OF Seiya Suzuki
Projected deal: 4 years, $100 million ($25 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Seiya Suzuki is probably the best bat available in free agency. The 32-year-old outfielder has been a model of consistency for the Cubs, with at least 20 home runs and an .800-plus OPS in three straight seasons. He's a plus defender in right field, too, where he posted career-best metrics in 2026. Suzuki has a rocket-like arm and consistently holds runners from the back corner.
Plenty of teams will take an interest in Suzuki's right-handed power profile; he draws walks and operates with sage discipline in the batter's box, despite occasionally elevated strikeout numbers. In the end, Toronto represents the most logical intersection of need and financial firepower to outbid the field.
OF Randy Arozarena
Projected deal: 5 years, $110 million ($22 million AAV) with Philadelphia Phillies
Randy Arozarena set new career highs in average (.281), OPS (.865) and home runs (26) in his walk year, emerging as one of the few bright spots on an otherwise disappointing Mariners team. He's more adequate than exceptional with his glove, but Arozarena provides middle-order power and he's a great personality hire.
The Phillies need Arozarena's bat and competitive fire in equal measure, plus he can help to safely return Bryce Harper to first base next season. Philadelphia desperately needs a right-handed slugger behind Harper in the lineup; the ability to finally add some stability to the outfield depth chart, as opposed to a 2026 rewind of the Adolis García or Max Kepler situations, should greatly appeal to a desperate Dave Dombrowski.
3B Teruaki Sato
Projected deal: 3 years, $75 million ($25 million AAV) with New York Yankees
Teruaki Sato is the most accomplished international free agent hoping to come Stateside this offseason. An MVP candidate in Japan's NPB, Sato hit .306 this year with 39 home runs and a .991 OPS. There are swing-and-miss and defense concerns, not dissimilar to the vague uncertainties that tanked Munetaka Murakami's stock last winter. Murakami ended up on a two-year deal with the White Sox, which he immediately outperformed.
Sato's left-handed power and upside at 27 years old could mean his market flourishes. But, given the baked-in gambles that come with signing an international free agent, he could end up getting lowballed, much like Murakami. A three-year, $75 million contract gives Sato a nice payday upfront while still hedging against potential struggles with a short-term framework. The Yankees need an infield slugger and have the money to roll the dice, so to speak, on Sato's immense talent.
LHP Trevor Rogers
Projected deal: 3 years, $60 million ($20 million) with Baltimore Orioles
Trevor Rogers has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency over the years, but he's coming off of two strong campaigns in Baltimore — and he's only 28 years old, so there's room left to establish himself as more than a third or fourth starter type. He couldn't recapture the success of 2025, when Rogers returned from injury to post a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts, but his 4.03 ERA last season does not capture the strength of his stuff (3.60 xERA). Moreover, the career-high 30 starts and 169.2 innings pitched was a nice addition to his résumé.
Teams will probably balk at dropping a full bag on Rogers' doorstep, ultimately, which opens the door for a short-term contract (probably with an opt-out clause or two) and a return to Baltimore. The Orioles need pitching badly and there are precious few better options than Rogers floating around the open market. This contract could turn into a total bargain.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Projected deal: 4 years, $84 million ($21 million AAV) with Chicago Cubs
Freddy Peralta's walk year has been a roller coaster of emotions. He bombed in New York after the Mets dealt multiple top-100 prospects to acquire him in an offseason trade. Then, after relocating to Tampa at the trade deadline, Peralta started slow before gradually picking up steam in September. Down the stretch and into the playoffs, he has looked more like the Cy Young candidate we witnessed in Milwaukee last season.
Peralta has not made the strongest case to prospective suitors in 2026, so a one-year, high-AAV deal to "prove it" is on the table. Ultimately, however, the 30-year-old should still be able to coax a substantial multi-year offer out of a desperate contender. His longtime NL Central rivals, the Cubs, are one such desperate contender. Peralta could join with the now-healthy Cade Horton and Justin Steele to revitalize Chicago's World Series hopes for 2027.
C Ryan Jeffers
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Minnesota Twins
The catcher market is tough to project, as there are so few who can hit like Ryan Jeffers. He was excellent in Minnesota this season, with 14 home runs and an .814 OPS in roughly half a season. He's the best catcher on the market, but Jeffers is not exactly lauded for his defense nor his game management behind the plate. He is not without injury concerns either, while even the best catchers end up in a timeshare eventually (especially when, like Jeffers, their glovework can be problematic).
Since there is such an absence of reliable hitters at the catcher position, Jeffers should be able to land a solid multi-year deal in the middle of his prime. A return to the Twins should not be discounted, even with Eduardo Tait and Vahn Lackey coming up through the Minors on accelerated timelines. Minnesota made a conscious decision not to trade him at the deadline, after all. The Twins would probably like to compete next season.
RHP Michael King
Projected deal: five years, $120 million ($24 million AAV) with San Diego Padres
Michael King returned to San Diego last winter on a backloaded three-year deal with opt outs. After an excellent showing in the playoffs, he will probably axe the remaining two years and $66 million on that contract in hopes of securing more guaranteed money this winter. King is not the sexiest name on the pitching market by any stretch, but he has made himself into a dependable workhorse with October equity.
The Padres clearly love King and new ownership, with their stated intention to build a contender, will probably consent to a reworked contract. San Diego has a paper-thin rotation as is. Losing King without a viable alternative in place could be disastrous, as the Padres don't have the trade ammo to compensate for a free agency exodus.
2B Brandon Lowe
Projected deal: 3 years, $66 million ($22 million AAV) with Pittsburgh Pirates
Brandon Lowe arrived in Pittsburgh via offseason trade and immediately became the most bankable presence in their lineup, with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and an .824 OPS. The 32-year-old can get in trouble with swing-and-miss, but he's a slugging outlier at second base. Moreover, Lowe quietly posted some of the best defensive metrics in MLB last season after struggling for years on the defensive end. It's fair to be skeptical about Lowe's ability to sustain this elite defense into his mid-30s, but he did everything he could to maximize his value as a free agent.
To that point, it's hard to imagine the Pirates letting Lowe walk without a fight. Pittsburgh threw more money around last offseason, with the front office clearly committed to changing their postseason fortunes. It did not come together in 2026, but Pittsburgh has a dangerous lineup and a very talented pitching staff. There's potential for a breakthrough in 2027, especially if Lowe sticks around.
LHP Adrián Morejón
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Adrián Morejón's mystery-shrouded absence in San Diego's NLDS loss to Milwaukee was a tough pill to swallow, but once again, the Padres end the season feeling like the second-best team in the National League. Part of the reason for San Diego's success this season, despite dramatic fluctuations from their lineup, was an elite bullpen. item.content:encoded:
After setting a franchise record with an MLB-best 103 wins in the 2026 regular season, the Brewers are vying for their first World Series appearance since 1982, which remains the only trip to the fall classic in franchise history.
Chourio pounced on the first pitch of Game 3 of the National League Championship Series from Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell, parking it over the right-center-field fence for a home run. It was his sixth career postseason dinger at just 22 years old, breaking a tie with Contreras -- who has three long balls in the 2026 playoffs -- for the most in Brewers postseason history.
With both in mind, who is each team’s all-time postseason home run king? Here’s a breakdown of the players who hold a franchise’s playoff home run record.
American League East
Blue Jays: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. -- 8
Vladdy put together one of the single greatest individual postseason performances we’ve ever seen in 2025, leading the Blue Jays all the way to Game 7 of the World Series. After starting his postseason career with six homer-less games, Guerrero hit all eight of his October long balls in ‘25. He surpassed José Bautista (six) for the most home runs in Blue Jays playoff history. The dinger that earned Guerrero the franchise lead came off of Shohei Ohtani in the World Series, no less.
Orioles: Frank Robinson -- 9
The Hall of Famer had a knack for the clutch. Robinson's 26 career walk-off hits (regular season and postseason) are the most by any player since RBI became official in 1920. That knack extended to the playoffs, where Robinson posted an .887 OPS and slammed 10 total homers, including a franchise-best nine with the Orioles. Robinson won World Series MVP in 1966 after hitting go-ahead home runs in Games 1 and 4 of a Baltimore sweep over the Dodgers.
Rays: Randy Arozarena -- 11
Arozarena put the Rays on his back in the 2020 postseason, recording 29 hits -- at the time the most in a single postseason. Ten of those hits were home runs, giving Arozarena another single-postseason record and pulling him ahead of Evan Longoria (nine) for the most playoff homers in Rays franchise history. Oh, and Arozarena did all of this as a rookie. He tagged one more postseason big fly with the Rays in '21 before joining the Mariners via trade in 2024.
Red Sox: David Ortiz -- 17
Big Papi was an October legend in the truest sense of the phrase. His walk-off heroics helped the Red Sox overcome a 3-0 series deficit in the 2004 ALCS, paving the way for a curse-breaking World Series title. Ortiz’s 17 playoff home runs included two walk-offs and six with the Red Sox facing elimination.
Yankees: Bernie Williams -- 22
Williams played in the postseason in 12 consecutive years from 1995-2006, with huge moments at several turns. His 1996 performance -- an 1.142 OPS with six homers -- is one of the best postseasons of all time. Overall, his 22 long balls are fifth most by any player in playoff history, sharing a list with other Yankees legends like Derek Jeter (20) and Mickey Mantle (18).
AL Central
Guardians: Jim Thome -- 17
Thome hit all 17 of his postseason homers with Cleveland. He’s one of three players with multiple postseason grand slams, along with Francisco Lindor and Jason Varitek. Thome's grand slams came in Game 6 of the 1998 ALCS against the Yankees and Game 2 of the 1999 ALDS against the Red Sox.
Royals: George Brett -- 10
Brett is one of just 12 players who have hit three home runs in a single postseason game. His herculean effort came in Game 3 of the 1978 ALCS against the Yankees. Even though in defeat, Brett memorably whacked three pitches over the fence, one out to left field, one over the center-field fence, and one to right field.
Tigers: Miguel Cabrera -- 9
Cabrera’s most memorable postseason may have come as a rookie with the championship-winning Marlins in 2003 (more on that soon). But his most impactful playoff performance happened in 2011, when he launched four home runs with a 1.261 OPS in 11 games for the Tigers. He later passed Delmon Young’s eight career playoff home runs as a Tiger with a solo shot in Game 1 of the 2014 ALDS.
Twins: Kirby Puckett -- 5
Goose Goslin is the Twins' franchise leader in postseason home runs with seven, but Puckett holds the record since the club moved to Minnesota in 1961. Puckett took two trips to the postseason with the Twins, winning the World Series both times (1987 and 1991). The Hall of Famer was particularly impactful in ‘91, when he hit four dingers on an overall .333/.396/.667 slash line. That included an iconic 11th-inning walk-off homer in Game 6 of the Fall Classic.
White Sox: Paul Konerko -- 7
Konerko mashed five of his seven postseason homers during Chicago's 2005 title run, narrowly besting teammate Paul Crede (four HR) for the franchise lead. Konerko hit two of his long balls while earning ALCS MVP honors, then later launched a go-ahead grand slam in Game 2 of the World Series to down the Astros.
AL West
Angels: Troy Glaus -- 9
Glaus hit seven of his nine postseason homers with the Angels during the club's World Series campaign in 2022. Three of those were go-ahead long balls in the sixth inning or later, which is tied with the Astros' Yordan Alvarez (2022) for the most such home runs in a single postseason.
Athletics: José Canseco -- 7
In addition to holding the club's all-time postseason home run record, Canseco holds a share of the record for the most homers in a single postseason by an A's player. He slugged four big flies in 1988, helping lead the Athletics to the AL Pennant. Two years later, Canseco passed Al Simmons for the most postseason home runs in A's franchise history with a dinger in Game 2 of the 1990 World Series.
Astros: Jose Altuve -- 28
Altuve added to his stature as one of baseball's best postseason hitters in 2026. He clubbed a solo shot in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series against the White Sox, putting him one home run behind Manny Ramirez for most all-time. And Altuve tends to meet the moment, too: A whopping 14 of his playoff homers have been of the game-tying or go-ahead variety, the most such homers in postseason history.
Mariners: Jay Buhner and Edgar Martinez -- 8
Buhner and Martinez each starred for the Mariners during the most successful era in franchise history, as the club made the playoffs four times between 1994 and 2001. Buhner took the early lead in career postseason homers, hitting four in ‘95 and two more in ‘97. But Martinez caught up to his longtime teammate in 2001 with a pair of long balls in the 2001 ALDS.
Rangers: Nelson Cruz -- 14
Cruz authored a historic postseason moment when he hit the first walk-off grand slam in postseason history in Game 2 of the 2011 ALCS against the Tigers. It remains one of just two walk-off postseason slams after Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman also accomplished the feat in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. Cruz, the owner of 464 regular-season home runs, hit his last postseason homer at age 41 with the Rays, becoming the second-oldest player to go yard in a playoff game.
National League East
Braves: Chipper Jones -- 13
Jones starred for an Atlanta team that made 11 consecutive postseason appearances from 1995-2005. The eight-time All-Star broke onto the October stage in a big way in ‘95, slugging two home runs -- including the game-winning shot in the ninth inning -- in a 5-4 win over the Rockies in Game 1 of the NLDS. Jones and Austin Riley are the only two players in Braves history with multiple go-ahead homers in the eighth inning or later of a postseason game.
Marlins: Miguel Cabrera -- 4
A 20-year-old, baby-faced Cabrera looked at home in his first postseason in 2003, steering the Florida Marlins to the franchise’s second World Series title. Cabrera launched four home runs in the ‘03 playoffs -- his only with the Marlins -- which stands as the most home runs in a single postseason at age 20 or younger in MLB history. With a long ball off Yankees right-hander Roger Clemens in Game 4 of the World Series, Cabrera became the second youngest player to go yard in the Fall Classic.
Mets: Daniel Murphy -- 7
All seven of Murphy’s playoff home runs with the Mets came during a magical two-week stretch in 2015. The second baseman homered in six straight postseason games -- spanning Game 4 of the NLDS through Game 4 of the NLCS -- to steer the Mets to the NL Pennant. That’s the longest streak in a single postseason in MLB history. Even more impressive, Murphy homered off three former Cy Young winners: Clayton Kershaw, Zack Greinke and Jake Arrieta.
Nationals: Bryce Harper, Juan Soto, Anthony Rendon and Ryan Zimmerman -- 5
Four of the most iconic players in Nationals franchise history (since the team moved from Montreal to Washington) share this distinction. Youth is a popular theme here. At 19 years old and 362 days, Harper became the second-youngest player in MLB history to homer in a postseason game when he went deep in Game 5 of the 2012 NLDS. Seven years later, Soto (20 years, 346 days) became the sixth-youngest player to homer in the playoffs, teeing off for a two-run shot in Game 3 of the 2019 NLDS.
Phillies: Kyle Schwarber -- 13
Schwarber is one of the most prolific power hitters in playoff history: His 24 career playoff home runs rank third most all time, trailing only Ramirez and Altuve. He’s crushed 15 homers in a Phillies uniform, the latest being a 447-foot shot in Game 2 of the 2026 NL Wild Card Series against the Braves. In 2022, Schwarber keyed a stirring run to the World Series with three home runs in the NLCS against the Padres and three more dingers in the Fall Classic against the Astros.
NL Central
Brewers: Jackson Chourio -- 6
Chourio tattooed a pair of home runs to help the Brewers stave off elimination in Game 2 of the 2024 NL Wild Card Series, becoming the second-youngest player in postseason history with a multi-HR game (20 years & 205 days). He’s the only player in postseason history with a leadoff home run under age 22 -- which he’s done three times -- and the only player in MLB history with six playoff home runs before turning 23. Chourio's leadoff dinger off Blake Snell in Game 3 of the NLCS against the Dodgers as his latest feat of strength.
Cardinals: Albert Pujols -- 13
Who else but The Machine? Pujols slugged 19 career playoff home runs -- T-7th most all time -- including 13 with the Cardinals. The future Hall of Famer tagged Randy Johnson for his first career playoff homer in Game 2 of the 2001 NLDS, a surefire sign of things to come. Pujols is one of just 12 players to go deep three times in a postseason game, doing so in Game 3 of the 2011 World Series. He also launched one of the most iconic home runs in franchise history with a go-ahead, three-run shot onto the train tracks in Houston off All-Star closer Brad Lidge in Game 5 of the 2005 NLCS.
Cubs: Kris Bryant, Anthony Rizzo and Kyle Schwarber -- 6
Talk about a fitting trio: These three All-Stars propelled the Cubs to a curse-breaking, legacy-defining World Series title in 2016. Bryant (2) and Rizzo (1) each launched home runs in the Fall Classic, keying victories in Games 5 and 6 to spur a historic 3-1 series comeback. Schwarber, one of the best postseason power hitters of all time, launched six of his 24 playoff homers with the Cubs, including five dingers in his introduction to playoff baseball in 2015.
Pirates: Willie Stargell -- 7
The Hall of Fame slugger managed just two home runs while hitting .217 across his first 26 postseason games, spanning five different playoff appearances. But Stargell flipped the script in his age-39 season in 1979, smashing five home runs while earning NLCS and World Series MVP honors. Stargell’s two-run blast in the sixth inning of Game 7 of the ‘79 World Series proved to be the World Series-winning hit.
Reds: Johnny Bench -- 10
Bench played in 10 postseason series across his illustrious 17-year career and, rather remarkably, homered in all but one of them -- only going without a long ball in the 1975 NLCS. The Hall of Fame catcher’s only multi-HR playoff series came in the 1976 Fall Classic, when he swatted a pair of homers, posted a 1.667 OPS and took home World Series MVP honors for the Big Red Machine.
NL West
D-backs: Chris Young -- 5
Young only played in 12 postseason games for Arizona, but that was plenty of time to rewrite the franchise record books. His leadoff home run in Game 3 of the 2007 NLDS against the Cubs’ Rich Hill accounts for the only leadoff home run in D-backs franchise history. Four years later, Young slammed a pair of long balls in Game 4 of the NLDS against the Brewers. It remains the only multi-HR game by a Diamondbacks’ hitter in franchise history.
Dodgers: Max Muncy -- 19
Muncy homered three times in the 2026 NLDS against the Braves, pushing his total to 19 playoff home runs and extending the most in Dodgers postseason history. It’s a remarkable record for Muncy to hold, given his journey: He first joined the Dodgers organization on a Minor League contract in 2017, after he was released by the Athletics. The three-time All-Star owns some of the most important home runs in Dodgers history. That includes his 18th-inning walk-off in Game 3 of the 2018 World Series and his eighth-inning home run in Game 7 of the 2025 Fall Classic, which set the stage for a stirring late-game comeback.
Giants: Barry Bonds -- 8
Bonds made the postseason only four times in 15 seasons with the Giants. And while he launched more home runs (756) than anyone in baseball history, Bonds actually was held without a home run in three of those four trips to October. All eight of his playoff home runs with San Francisco came in 2002, when he posted a 1.559 OPS in 17 games while leading the Giants to the NL Pennant. The most memorable occurred in the ninth inning of Game 2 of the World Series, when he clobbered a blast to right field off closer Troy Percival. Arozarena (10, 2020 Rays) is the only player with more home runs in a single postseason.
Padres: Manny Machado -- 9
Machado extended his own franchise record in his first at-bat of the 2026 postseason, launching a home run in the first inning of Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series against the Cubs’ Matthew Boyd. Machado ushered in a new era of baseball in San Diego when he signed a 10-year deal ahead of the 2019 season, and the Padres have made the playoffs in five of the eight years since. The seven-time All-Star was at his best in the 2022 playoffs, helping San Diego win a pair of postseason series thanks to four home runs in 12 games.
Rockies: Matt Holliday -- 5
Holliday is responsible for one of the defining moments in Rockies history, although it has nothing to do with a home run: He belly-flopped into home plate to score the game-winning run in Game 163 in 2007, giving Colorado the Wild Card tiebreaker over San Diego. That mad dash set the stage for Holliday's only postseason stint with the club, which was wildly successful. The seven-time All-Star homered in each of his first two playoff games in the NLDS against the Phillies, and wound up with five long balls as the Rockies earned the franchise’s first World Series berth.

item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Guardians wouldn't be heading into Game 2 of the ALCS with a 1-0 series lead over the Tampa Bay Rays if it weren't for the heroics that superstar Jose Ramirez has put on all October long.
Going back to the final three games of the ALDS, and now Game 1 of the ALCS, Ramirez has simply put Cleveland's lineup on his back.
Terry Francona set it when he managed, and Stephen Vogt has echoed it: when Hosey goes, the Guardians go.
Ramirez is doing more than just swinging a hot bat right now; he's also setting Cleveland franchise history with how much success he's had at the plate so far this postseason.
In the top of the ninth inning on Monday night, Ramirez worked Cole Sulser into a 3-2 count with two outs and Angel Martinez standing on second base. The Tampa Bay pitcher left a cutter up in the zone, and Ramirez took it the other way
Martinez crossed home plate, and the floodgates opened for Cleveland to score two more runs and seal the deal for the Guardians in Game 1.
Looking back to Ramirez, though, this was his eighth hit and eighth RBI of the postseason up to this point.
Ramirez also tied a Cleveland franchise record, becoming just the third player to log an RBI in four straight playoff games. The other two were Jim Thome in 1998-99 and Sandy Alomar in 1997, who still coaches first base for the Guardians.
Ramirez is already one of, if not the best, players in franchise history.
That said, considering the legendary players who played for Cleveland in the 90s, like Albert Belle and Manny Ramirez, along with impressive offensive players in the late 2010s, like Francisco Lindor and Michael Brantley, it really shows how amazing Ramirez is doing.
Whether it's smacking home runs or just getting the ball in play, Vogt said after Game 1 that Ramirez just has a knack for getting on base and making things happen. There's nowhere in the box score or in a stat to measure that impact, but it's real, and the Guardians are feeling it right now.
Vogt went on to talk about how Ramirez's energy "100 percent" feeds off the rest of the team.
Who knows what will happen throughout the rest of the series, but the Guardians should be in a good spot to win the ALCS if Ramirez continues to play at this level.

While Francisco Lindor’s baseball career has made him one of the most recognizable players on the New York Mets, his life away from the diamond has become an equally important part of his public story. Puerto Rican shortstop reached another career milestone on September 27, 2026, hitting his 300th career home run against the Washington Nationals. The feat also made him just the 11th switch-hitter in MLB history to reach the 300 home run mark, and the second, behind Carlos Beltran, to combine that feat with at least 200 stolen bases.
Off the field, Lindor is married to his wife, Katia Reguero. The couple are proud parents of three children. The couple met on Instagram in 2020, before marrying in December 2021, and now share children Kalina Zoé, 3, and Amapola Chloé, 2, and son Koa Amani, 1. Reguero has also developed her own public persona through music, parenting talks and community work.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s family life beyond Mets stardom
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero have raised a family and juggled the demanding schedule that comes with Major League Baseball. Lindor’s career involves plenty of travel, a long regular season and public scrutiny at all times, while Reguero has built her own professional and creative interests.
The couple have three children, Kalina Zoé born in November 2020, Amapola Chloé born in June 2023, and Koa Amani born in March 2025. Koa was born in the middle of the MLB season, and Lindor returned to the New York Mets shortly after his son’s birth. MLB said the Mets were preparing to play the Miami Marlins the following day, and Lindor was with the team.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s marriage and children
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero's relationship began online in early 2020. Lindor messaged Reguero on Instagram, and they talked for about three months before meeting in person in Arizona. They ended up getting married, and their relationship blossomed as Lindor continued his baseball career.
The couple said "I do" on December 16, 2021, at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens in Miami, Florida. Their marriage came after they already had Kalina, giving the family a personal foundation before their wedding.
As Lindor’s career has progressed, so have family milestones. Lindor went back to be with Reguero when Koa was born in March 2025 and returned to the Mets. The moment illustrated how a player at the highest level can have family obligations and a demanding baseball schedule intersect.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s lives beyond baseball
Lindor is more than his stats and his accomplishments with the New York Mets. His work with youth clinics, Boys & Girls Clubs and the Lindor Smiles community initiative is noted in MLB’s official profile, as well as a scholarship fund he created at Montverde Academy and a $1 million donation to the school’s Lindor Hall project.
Katia Reguero has also kept up interests outside of being Lindor’s wife. She has a background in music and has become known for her podcast and advocacy work in parenting. She also got noticed in 2026 playing the national anthem on violin at a New York Mets game, bringing another facet of her identity into the baseball environment around her family.
In September 2026, Lindor hit his 300th career home run, another milestone in his baseball career. Off the field, though, his life is one of marriage, three children, involvement in the community, and a wife who has built a public career in her own right. All of those factors combine to give a broader picture of the New York Mets star than just being an MLB shortstop.

Francisco Lindor’s evolution from an eighth overall pick in the MLB Draft to one of baseball’s highest-paid shortstops has seen several stages of financial growth. Lindor, who made a name for himself with Cleveland, arrived with the New York Mets prior to the 2021 season and quickly became a center of attention for the franchise.
The Mets then gave Lindor a 10-year, $341 million extension that will keep him in New York through 2031. The deal included a $21 million signing bonus, performance incentives, no-trade protection and $50 million in deferred payments. And with his previous MLB contracts, the deal changed the financial scale of Lindor’s career.
Francisco Lindor’s Mets $341 million contract keeps New York star tied to Queens through 2031
In 2021, the New York Mets acquired Francisco Lindor from Cleveland and signed him to a 10-year, $341 million extension. The deal is worth an average of $34.1 million a year and extends through the 2031 season.

| Average annual value | $34.1 million |
| Signing bonus | $21 million |

| Deferred money | $50 million |
| Free agency | 2032 |
The pact also includes broad trade protection. Lindor had a 15-team no-trade clause from 2021-25, then a complete no-trade clause from 2026-31.
A big item is the $50 million in deferred compensation. Lindor will receive $5 million annually from 2032 to 2041, meaning payments will extend for a decade following the playing portion of the contract.
Francisco Lindor remains central to New York Mets' future
Lindor’s financial ascent started with Cleveland, which drafted him eighth overall in the 2011 MLB Draft. His initial signing bonus was reported at $2.9 million before his earnings through pre-arbitration and arbitration contracts increased.

This progression shows how Lindor’s salary went up as his standing in MLB grew. He was a four-time All-Star and two-time Gold Glove winner when he arrived in New York.
Francisco Lindor’s $341 million deal details explained
Lindor’s deal also includes extra money tied to individual achievements, giving him a chance to add to his guarantyd earnings.

The $341 million guarantee is one aspect of Lindor’s financial picture that is part of the contract structure. His salary from the Cleveland team and the 2021 Mets, and his signing bonus and performance incentives contributed to the increase of his fortune in MLB.
The 2026 contract data provided has Lindor with a payroll figure of $34.1 million and $27 million in cash compensation. The same annual payroll number is listed through 2031, when his playing contract is up.
Thus, Francisco Lindor’s financial path has taken him from his initial Cleveland contract to one of the largest commitments in New York Mets history. The $341 million extension gives him long-term security, and the deferred payments and incentives extend the financial impact of the agreement well beyond his final contracted season.

The 2026 MLB season is over for the New York Mets, and now they are in offseason mode. One major question mark hanging over the Mets is whether or not infielder Bo Bichette will opt out of his contract.
Bichette’s current contract with the Mets sees him earn $42 million per year over the next two years, per Spotrac. Nonetheless, the question is whether the veteran produced enough this season for another team to pay him more.
In the 2026 season, a batting average of .260 with 166 hits, 18 home runs, 78 RBIs, and 76 runs scored in 160 games, per StatMuse. With an offseason decision looming for Bichette, SNY’s MLB insider Chelsea Janes shared her outlook on how this situation will play out.
“[Juan Soto] and [Francisco] Lindor certainly talked like guys who really wanted Bo Bichette back and have probably communicated that to him,” Janes said during a Sept. 28 appearance on “Baseball Night in New York.”
“I think Bo Bichette stays. I expect him and his agent to kind of let it play out a little bit, make it seem like they get a feel for the market, just kind of make sure that no one’s going to change his thinking.”
Insider Shares Few Other Reasons Bo Bichete Will Stay
Moreover, aside from Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor potentially being in Bichette’s ear telling him to stay, Janes also noted two other reasons why she believes the Mets infielder will remain in New York and not opt out of his contract.
“He settled in here, and he came here for a reason,” Janes added. “I believe what Bo Bichette said early on, that he understands what New York is, and he wants to succeed here. So I think he’s now comfortable. Frankly, his numbers just weren’t that good. It’s not a platform year. So it was $42 million and try again. I think it’s now a bit of a no-brainer.”
Bo Bichette Urged to Remain With Mets for 2027 Season
Recently, John Harper of SNY urged Bichette to remain with the Mets and not opt out of his contract. Harper believes that if the infielder decides to test the market again, no team will give him more than the $42 million per year he’s earning in New York.
Moreover, there’s a potential lockout looming, so it might be in Bichette’s interest to stay with the Mets and possibly test the market next year if he has a better season, given that his three-year contract has opt-outs after each of the first two seasons.
“You’ve got the lockout coming,” Harper said in a Sept. 11 video on SNY’s YouTube channel. “You’re not sure what the salary structure is going to look like, if there’s a cap or not. I think that’s part of it too. [Bichette] has been good since the terrible start, but I was looking at it, and he’s not a superstar. He’s a really good offensive player [and] has got an under .800 OPS in the second half, when he’s done most of his best hitting.
“He doesn’t hit for a lot of power [and] he’s been a clutch guy again since the bad start, hitting almost .300 with runners in scoring position. To me, [$84 million] for the next two years; you can go out in the market after that [but] you’re not getting [$42 million] a year anymore. Now you’re getting a longer contract, but I would stick it out for these two years and then maybe take my chance.”

item.content:encoded:
- MLB. La última apertura de Justin Verlander marca el final de una carrera brillante
- MLB. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. consigue uno de los sencillos productores más extraños del béisbol
Los New York Mets no solo se quedaron fuera de los playoffs en 2026. Se desplomaron. Con un récord de 74-88, un último lugar en la División Este de la Liga Nacional y una de las nóminas más altas de las Grandes Ligas, la temporada terminó siendo un completo fracaso. Las lesiones, una construcción deficiente del roster y el bajo rendimiento general fueron factores importantes, por lo que no toda la responsabilidad puede recaer sobre dos jugadores.
Sin embargo, la rendición de cuentas debe comenzar con quienes estaban llamados a liderar al equipo. Francisco Lindor debía ser el corazón de la franquicia, mientras que Jorge Polanco llegó como un bateador veterano confiable. En cambio, ambos terminaron simbolizando una campaña en la que el talento más caro y probado estuvo muy lejos de responder a las expectativas de Nueva York.
Francisco Lindor nunca jugó como la estrella franquicia que esperaban los Mets
Lindor merece cierto contexto. Se sometió a una cirugía en el codo durante el invierno, sufrió una fractura del hueso ganchoso de la mano durante los entrenamientos y posteriormente estuvo cerca de dos meses fuera por una distensión en la pantorrilla. Con tantas interrupciones, encontrar ritmo fue prácticamente imposible.
Aun así, los Mets necesitaban una superestrella, no solo un jugador disponible en la alineación, y pocas veces la tuvieron. Lindor bateó para .225, con un porcentaje de embasado (.309), slugging (.423) y un OPS de .732, el más bajo de toda su carrera. Conectó 21 cuadrangulares, pero apenas produjo 49 carreras impulsadas en 105 juegos.
Su retroceso no se limitó al bate. Cometió 11 errores, la mayor cifra de su carrera, y terminó por debajo del promedio en la métrica Outs Above Average de Statcast. Un análisis sobre el rendimiento de los Mets de un año a otro mostró que su aporte cayó de 6.1 WAR en 2025 a una proyección de apenas 1.9 WAR en 2026, la mayor disminución entre las principales figuras que regresaron al equipo.
Nada de esto convierte a Lindor en un mal jugador, y las lesiones fueron un factor real. Pero cuando una franquicia está construida alrededor de un campocorto superestrella, perder más de cuatro victorias de valor esperado puede hundir una temporada. Los Mets confiaban en tener una ventaja clara en el shortstop y terminaron sin estabilidad ni excelencia en ambos lados del terreno.
Jorge Polanco fue el mayor problema de la alineación
Si Lindor representó la mayor decepción por las expectativas que existían sobre él, Jorge Polanco fue quien más perjudicó al equipo por sus resultados. Los Mets le otorgaron un contrato de dos años y 40 millones de dólares después de que conectara 26 cuadrangulares y registrara un OPS de .821 con Seattle en 2025, esperando que aportara profundidad y poder al lineup.
Lo que recibieron fue una de las peores temporadas ofensivas de todo el béisbol: promedio de .148, porcentaje de embasado de .201, slugging de .230, apenas dos jonrones y seis carreras impulsadas en 145 apariciones al plato. Además, fue utilizado casi exclusivamente como bateador designado, por lo que tampoco pudo compensar su bajo rendimiento con el guante. Tanto FanGraphs como Baseball Reference lo evaluaron con -1.4 WAR pese a disputar un número limitado de juegos.
Las lesiones en la muñeca, el tendón de Aquiles y el tobillo lo acompañaron durante toda la campaña, hasta que una cirugía en el tobillo puso fin a su temporada en agosto. Eso explica parte del desplome, pero no su impacto. Un bateador designado existe para producir ofensivamente, y Polanco ocupó un lugar en la alineación sin aportar poder, promedio ni capacidad para embasarse.
La oficina principal también merece críticas por construir un roster frágil, y las lesiones nunca dejaron de aparecer. Aun así, Lindor y Polanco sobresalen porque su producción estuvo muy por debajo del rol que debían desempeñar. La falta de liderazgo de Lindor le quitó a los Mets la base de su proyecto, mientras que el bate de Polanco convirtió una de las principales inversiones del invierno en un peso muerto. Ellos no fueron los únicos responsables de las 88 derrotas, pero sí representan mejor que nadie por qué un equipo diseñado para competir terminó hundido en el último lugar.

item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to this season’s final edition of Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
TUESDAY
With his 25th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing broke Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
Kodai Senga became one of just 11 Japanese-born players to reach eight career saves, joining: Kazuhiro Sasaki (129), Koji Uehara (95), Takashi Saito (84), Akinori Otsuka (39), Shigetoshi Hasegawa (33), Shingo Takatsu (27), Hideki Irabu (16), Hisanori Takahashi (10), Masanori Murakami (9), and Yoshihisa Hirano (8).
Francisco Alvarez and Carson Benge each hit two doubles, marking the first time multiple Mets hit multiple doubles in a game since Ronny Mauricio and Jeff McNeil did it on July 27, 2025, in San Francisco.
WEDNESDAY
Marcus Semien hit his 15th home run of the year, giving the Mets six or more players with 15+ homers for the fifth time in franchise history after 2000 (7), 2017 (8), 2019 (6), and 2025 (6). The only teams with more 15-homer players this season were the Cubs, Reds, and Dodgers (all tied at 7). Of the Mets’ players with 15+ homers last season and this season, only two (Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto) overlap.
Juan Soto reached base four times for the 103rd time in his career, moving past Ted Williams for the third-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Mickey Mantle (121) and Jimmie Foxx (112).
Soto became the fifth Met to get intentionally walked three times in a game, after Claudell Washington (August 26, 1980), Vince Coleman (August 10, 1992), Todd Hundley (June 28, 1997), and David Wright (May 19, 2007, and July 18, 2009).
Brett Baty’s 455-foot home run tied the longest blast of his big league career, a homer off Brad Lord on August 20, 2025, in Washington.
Francisco Alvarez’s seventh-inning single registered an exit velocity of 113.7 mph. It was Alvarez’s 15th career batted ball with an exit velocity of 112+ mph, the second-most by a Met player in the Statcast era (since 2015) behind Pete Alonso, who had a whopping 130.
Alvarez, Lindor, and Baty each recorded a batted ball with an exit velocity over 110 mph, marking the first time the Mets recorded three batted balls with an exit velocity of 110+ mph in the same game since September 10, 2025, in Philadelphia.
Nolan McLean completed his rookie year with a total of 179.2 innings pitched, the most by a Mets rookie since Jae Weong Seo (188.1 in 2003), and 194 strikeouts, the third-most by a Mets rookie behind Dwight Gooden (276 in 1984) and Kodai Senga (202 in 2023).
McLean recorded his 250th strikeout in his 39th career game, tying Jacob deGrom for the fifth-fewest games by a Met to reach that milestone behind Dwight Gooden (29 games), Matt Harvey (34 games), Noah Syndergaard (36 games), and Kodai Senga (38 games).
McLean recorded his 26th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since deGrom (29) and Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
McLean became the first rookie with 20 quality starts since the Royals’ Yordano Ventura (22 in 2014). McLean’s 20 quality starts this season were tied with Sonny Gray and Cam Schlittler for fifth-most in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (22), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (22), Sandy Alcantara (21), and Michael Wacha (21). McLean also recorded his 21st start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
THURSDAY
Zac Thornton’s 63 strikeouts through 15 career games ranks fourth among Mets left-handers, behind Steven Matz (87), Bill Pulsipher (74), and David Peterson (69).
Juan Soto became the second Mets player to get intentionally walked four times in a two-game span, after Travis d’Arnaud did it while batting in the No. 8 spot ahead of Jon Niese and Bartolo Colón on June 1-2, 2014, in Philadelphia.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 63rd time this season. That ties 2013 for the most such games the Mets have had in a season in the Wild-Card Era (since 1995).
Over the franchise’s first five trips to Arlington, the Mets are still yet to lose a series on the road against the Rangers. They won two of three in 2003, won two of three in 2011, split a two-game set in 2017, won two out of three in 2024, and won two out of three again in 2026.
FRIDAY
Carson Benge became the first Mets rookie with 20+ homers and 20+ stolen bases in a season.
Benge became just the eighth player in MLB history to join the 20/20 club in their debut season, joining: Jackson Chourio (2024), Anthony Volpe (2023), Bobby Witt Jr. (2022), Julio Rodríguez (2022), Marty Cordova (1995), Ellis Burks (1987), and Mitchell Page (1977). (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Benge recorded his 43rd multi-hit game of the season, breaking Pete Alonso’s 2019 record for the most multi-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
With a pinch-hit single in the eighth inning, Brett Baty extended his career-high 18-game on-base streak. It was snapped with an 0-for-4 performance on Saturday.
Bo Bichette hit his fourth home run at Nationals Park this season, tied for the most by a Mets player in any season on the road against the Nats/Expos. His six extra-base hits trail only David Wright (7) in 2012.
Francisco Lindor didn’t notch his 300th home run on Friday night, but he did record three batted balls in a game at 107+ mph for the first time in the Statcast era (since 2015). Unfortunately for him, only one of the three resulted in a base hit.
The Mets allowed five wild pitches in a game and four wild pitches in an inning for the first time in franchise history.
SATURDAY
Jonah Tong set career highs with nine strikeouts and 19 whiffs in a game.
Mets pitchers recorded 14 or more strikeouts in a game for the 12th time this season, the fourth-most such games in a season in franchise history behind 2021 (19), 2019 (17), and 2022 (17).
With a start at shortstop, Brett Baty became the first Mets player to play six different positions in a season since Jeff McNeil in 2023.
Nate Lavender has recorded 19 scoreless appearances in his first 21 career outings, tied with Jaime Cerda, Erik Goeddel, and Daniel Zamora for the second-most by a Met behind Joe Smith (20).
In the Mets’ penultimate game of the season, their No. 8 and No. 9 hitters hit back-to-back homers (A.J. Ewing and Ronny Mauricio). The 2026 Mets had done that once before — in their first game of the season, when Carson Benge and Francisco Alvarez went deep at Citi Field against the Pirates.
The Mets clinched their sixth consecutive victory in the season series with Washington. Their record against the Nationals is 57-33 over that span.
SUNDAY
Francisco Lindor became the fifth player to hit their 300th career home run while having played at least 50% of their games at shortstop, joining Ernie Banks, Cal Ripken Jr., Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Tejada. (source: Sarah Langs on X) He is also the 11th switch-hitter to reach the 300-homer mark. (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Lindor became one of 27 players with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, and the third active player to have reached the milestone along with Andrew McCutchen and Mike Trout. He is the fifth member of that club to have played for the Mets; the others were Willie Mays, Darryl Strawberry, Gary Sheffield, and Carlos Beltrán.
Lindor became the seventh player to hit their 300th home run as a Met, joining Dave Kingman, George Foster, Gary Carter, Mike Piazza, Mo Vaughn, and Curtis Granderson.
Lindor’s 300th homer registered a 110.8-mph exit velocity, marking the third-hardest-hit homer as a right-handed batter in his career. His only harder-hit homer from the right side as a Met came on another afternoon in Washington, when he took MacKenzie Gore deep on August 21, 2025.
Ronny Maurcio became the first Met to hit three consecutive homers out of the No. 9 spot, with two on Saturday and one on Sunday. (source: SNY broadcast)
Carson Benge recorded his 14th three-hit game of the season, extending his record for the most three-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
Juan Soto holds a 1.101 OPS against the Nationals in 39 games played facing his former team. That’s the third-highest OPS for any player with at least 150 plate appearances against the Nationals/Expos, trailing only Jim Edmonds (1.198) and Todd Helton (1.114).
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Let’s talk about the rookies.
In Carson Benge, Nolan McLean, A.J. Ewing, and Zac Thornton, the Mets have four rookies with at least 1.5 bWAR*. That’s tied for the most rookies with 1.5+ bWAR* in a season in franchise history, matching the mark from 1983 (Darryl Strawberry, Carlos Diaz, Walt Terrell, and Doug Sisk).
In Benge, McLean, and Ewing, the Mets have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*. Prior to this year, they had never had as many as two such rookies in a single season. In fact, the 2026 Mets are just the third team in the modern era (since 1900) to have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*, joining:
2006 Marlins (4: Hanley Ramírez, Dan Uggla, Josh Johnson, and Aníbal Sánchez)
1989 Orioles (3: Randy Milligan, Bob Milacki, Gregg Olson)
*bWAR separated for position players and pitchers, not cumulative
Thank you for following along all year! Here’s to many more stat parties in 2027…

item.content:encoded:
Juan Soto did not need a long answer when asked why the New York Mets can contend in 2027. After a 74-88 season that kept them out of the MLB playoffs, Soto gave a two-word answer: Carson Benge.
That is quite an endorsement for a rookie who just finished his first major league season.
The Mets entered 2026 with much bigger expectations, but injuries and an inconsistent roster eventually caught up with them. They finished last in the NL East and missed the postseason for the second straight year.
Benge, however, gave the club something it desperately needed: a reason to look forward.
The rookie finished with a .282 batting average, 20 home runs, 65 RBI, 168 hits and 22 stolen bases, according to the supplied 2026 statistics. SNY also reported that Benge became the first Mets rookie to reach 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases.
Juan Soto sees Carson Benge as part of the Mets’ future
Soto’s answer carries even more weight because he knows what the Mets need to fix.
The superstar played 111 games and hit .275 with 27 home runs, 68 RBI, a .393 on-base percentage and a .515 slugging percentage. But two calf injuries cost him significant time during the season, including a lengthy absence in July and August.
Soto has also said the Mets need to be active this offseason and add to their young core. He specifically pointed to Benge and other young players as reasons to believe the organization is moving in the right direction.
That puts plenty of attention on Benge heading into 2027. Not bad for a rookie who just finished his first trip around the league. Queens may have had a rough 2026, but at least Benge gave Mets fans something worth circling on the calendar.
The Mets still have work to do. Soto and Francisco Lindor provide veteran star power, but the pitching staff and overall roster need improvement after a 74-88 finish.
For now, though, Soto has made his choice clear when it comes to the biggest reason for optimism.
